day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Collect luggage, take the Metro (Linha Vermelha) from Aeroporto station to your accommodation for roughly €1.80, check in to Lisbon City Stay, and freshen up.
day_by_day.afternoon: Take a relaxed stroll through Baixa-Chiado, Lisbon's bustling downtown grid. Walk along Rua Augusta, cross the iconic Praça do Comércio by the Tagus riverfront, and soak in the city atmosphere. Entry to the square and riverside promenade is completely free. Get your bearings and pick up a 24-hour Viva Viagem transit card (€0.50 + €6.40 for unlimited rides) at any Metro station.
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Bairro Alto neighbourhood for dinner. Explore the lively streets and grab a budget-friendly meal at one of the many tascas (traditional taverns) offering a prato do dia (dish of the day) for €7–10, including bread, soup, main, and a glass of wine. Afterwards, enjoy a free evening walk along Rua do Carmo or sit at a miradouro (viewpoint) such as Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara to watch the city lights.

meals.breakfast: Grab a quick pastel de nata (custard tart, ~€1.20) and a bica (espresso, ~€0.80) at a café near the airport or upon arrival in the city centre.
meals.lunch: Pick up a bifana (pork sandwich, ~€2.50) or a tostas mistas from a local café near your hotel as a quick, cheap bite after check-in.
meals.dinner: Tasca dinner in Bairro Alto — prato do dia with soup, main course (e.g., bacalhau à brás or frango assado), bread, and house wine for €8–11 per person. Try Tasca do Chico or similar neighbourhood spots.

day_by_day.notes: Since your flight lands at 13:00, allow 1–1.5 hours for baggage, immigration, and transit to the hotel. Keep Day 1 light and exploratory. Validate your transit card every time you board. The Viva Viagem card works on Metro, buses, and trams.

day_by_day.morning: Join the Alfama Historic District Walking Tour — Lisbon's oldest Moorish neighbourhood with narrow medieval alleyways, colourful tiled buildings, and hidden viewpoints. Many free or low-cost guided tours run on a tip basis (budget €5–10 tip). Highlights include Largo das Portas do Sol viewpoint and the charming streets around the Sé Cathedral (free exterior, €3 interior).
day_by_day.afternoon: São Jorge Castle and Mouraria Exploration — walk up to the 11th-century Moorish castle perched atop Lisbon's highest hill. Entry to São Jorge Castle costs approximately €15 (check for discounts with Lisbon Card or student ID). Enjoy sweeping panoramic views of the city and the Tagus River. Afterwards, wander down into the Mouraria neighbourhood — Lisbon's multicultural heart — where entry is free and the atmosphere is vibrant.
day_by_day.evening: Experience authentic Fado music in Alfama. Many local restaurants and small venues offer free Fado performances in the evening — simply order dinner or a drink (budget €10–15). Alternatively, sit at Miradouro da Graça for a free sunset view before dinner.

meals.breakfast: Padaria (local bakery) near your hotel — fresh bread roll with butter and coffee for €2–3. Try a galão (milky coffee) for a true Lisbon morning.
meals.lunch: Grab a quick lunch in Alfama at a local tasca — caldo verde soup + grilled sardines or prego sandwich for around €8–10.
meals.dinner: Dinner in Mouraria — look for affordable Arabic-influenced or traditional Portuguese spots. A full meal with wine costs €10–13. Try O Corvo or similar neighbourhood restaurants.

day_by_day.notes: Wear comfortable walking shoes — Alfama and the castle area involve steep, cobblestone streets. Bring a water bottle. Saturday mornings can be busy; arrive at the walking tour meeting point 10 minutes early. Keep valuables secure in Alfama as it is a tourist-heavy area.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Feira da Ladra flea market in Campo de Santa Clara (open Tuesday and Saturday, so check if a special Sunday market is running — otherwise substitute with a morning visit to Museu do Azulejo, the National Tile Museum, entry ~€5). The tile museum is a hidden gem showcasing Portugal's iconic azulejo tradition across beautifully decorated rooms inside a 16th-century convent.
day_by_day.afternoon: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Experience — spend the afternoon at Lisbon's iconic food hall in Cais do Sodré. Sample the best of Portuguese cuisine from top local chefs at reasonable prices: a petisco (small plate) costs €3–7, meaning you can try 3–4 different dishes for under €20. Try piri-piri chicken, fresh seafood, ginjinha shots, and artisan cheeses. The market itself is free to enter.
day_by_day.evening: Sunset at Miradouro do Adamastor (Miradouro de Santa Catarina) — a popular free viewpoint loved by locals and students. Street musicians often perform here. Bring a bottle of local wine from a nearby supermarket (Minipreço or Pingo Doce, ~€3–5) and enjoy the Tagus River panorama. End the evening with a stroll along Cais do Sodré waterfront.

meals.breakfast: Café A Brasileira in Chiado (historic landmark café) — pastel de nata and coffee for €3–4. Enjoy it standing at the counter for the authentic local experience and lower price.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at Time Out Market — mix of small plates totalling €10–15, including a glass of wine or craft beer.
meals.dinner: Supermarket picnic or affordable restaurant near Cais do Sodré — pick up local cheese, chouriço, olives, bread, and wine from Pingo Doce for €8–10 total, and enjoy a riverside picnic, or dine at a neighbourhood restaurant for €10–13.

day_by_day.notes: Time Out Market is busiest between 13:00–15:00 on weekends — arrive slightly before or after the rush. Cais do Sodré Metro station is one stop from Baixa-Chiado, making it very accessible. Sunday may see reduced opening hours for some museums — always verify in advance.

day_by_day.morning: Day trip to Sintra — take the direct train from Rossio Station (€2.35 each way, ~40 minutes). Explore the UNESCO-listed historic centre of Sintra on foot: the colourful Palácio Nacional de Sintra (€10 entry) dominates the town centre with its iconic twin chimneys. Walk the charming village streets and browse local pastry shops for travesseiros (almond pastries, ~€1.50).
day_by_day.afternoon: Hike up to Pena Palace (€14 entry or view from outside for free) or the free Moorish Castle ruins for panoramic views over the Atlantic and surrounding forest. Pack a light snack from a local bakery to save money on the hilltop. Return to Lisbon by train in the late afternoon, arriving back with energy for the evening.
day_by_day.evening: Relaxed evening in Lisbon's Príncipe Real neighbourhood — one of the city's most elegant and local-feeling areas. Browse the weekend design market (if running) or simply enjoy the tree-lined square. Have dinner at a neighbourhood restaurant or pick up affordable food from a local mercearia (grocery-deli).

meals.breakfast: Quick breakfast at Rossio Station café before catching the train — coffee and toast for €2.50.
meals.lunch: Picnic in Sintra's park — buy a travesseiro pastry (~€1.50), local cheese, and fruit from village shops for under €6 total. Eat with views of the palace gardens.
meals.dinner: Dinner in Príncipe Real — try a neighbourhood tasca for a prato do dia at €9–12, or grab affordable mezze-style food from one of the area's casual eateries.

day_by_day.notes: Trains to Sintra run frequently from Rossio (every 20–30 minutes). Buy a return ticket at the station. Sintra involves significant uphill walking — wear sturdy shoes and bring sunscreen and water. To save on entry fees, the exterior views of Pena Palace from the Moorish Castle are stunning and free with the castle ticket (~€8).

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Feira da Ladra flea market at Campo de Santa Clara (open Tuesday mornings, free entry). Browse antiques, vintage ceramics, old books, and second-hand azulejo tiles. A great place to find affordable, authentic souvenirs — budget €5–20 depending on what you find. Nearby, the Panteão Nacional (National Pantheon) offers entry for ~€4 and rooftop views.
day_by_day.afternoon: Final exploration of Belém district — take Tram 15E or bus from Praça do Comércio (~€2 with Viva Viagem card). Visit the Jerónimos Monastery exterior (free) and the iconic Torre de Belém (€6 entry or admire from outside for free). Stop at the original Pastéis de Belém bakery for the world-famous custard tarts at €1.30 each — a Lisbon bucket-list experience. Walk along the Tagus riverfront promenade.
day_by_day.evening: Final dinner back in the city centre — splurge slightly on your last night with a full traditional Portuguese meal. Try a restaurant in Intendente or Martim Moniz neighbourhood for excellent value: grilled fish, açorda, or carne de porco à alentejana with wine for €13–18. Finish with a ginjinha (sour cherry liqueur, €1.50) at one of the tiny ginjinha bars near Rossio Square. Pack bags and prepare for departure.

meals.breakfast: Final Portuguese breakfast at a local café — galão, torrada (thick toast with butter), and a pastel de nata for €3.50.
meals.lunch: Lunch in Belém — pastéis de Belém (2 tarts, ~€2.60) plus a bifana or tostas from a nearby café for under €7 total.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner in Intendente or Martim Moniz — full traditional meal with wine for €14–18. End with ginjinha at Ginjinha Sem Rival near Rossio (€1.50 per shot).

day_by_day.notes: Feira da Ladra opens around 09:00 and winds down by 14:00 — go early for the best finds. Belém is about 6 km west of the city centre; the 15E tram is scenic but slow — bus 728 is faster. Check your flight details for Day 6 departure and arrange transport to the airport the night before. Metro to the airport costs €1.80 and takes about 25 minutes from the city centre.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Clear customs, collect luggage, and take the Aerobus or Metro (Red Line to Green Line) to central Lisbon. Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up.
day_by_day.afternoon: After settling in, take a leisurely stroll through the Baixa-Chiado neighborhood to get your bearings. Walk along Rua Augusta, cross the iconic Praça do Comércio by the Tagus River, and soak in the city atmosphere. Stop at a local pastelaria for a coffee and pastel de nata to kick off your Lisbon food journey.
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Time Out Market Lisbon Food Experience for your first proper meal in Lisbon. Sample a variety of Portuguese dishes — from grilled fish to petiscos (Portuguese tapas) — all under one roof. A perfect, low-pressure introduction to local cuisine after a travel day.

meals.breakfast: Eat before or during your flight — nothing scheduled pre-arrival.
meals.lunch: Light snack on arrival: coffee and pastel de nata at a Baixa pastelaria (€3–5).
meals.dinner: Time Out Market Lisbon — budget €20–30 per person sampling multiple stalls (bacalhau, bifanas, local cheeses, and a glass of wine).

day_by_day.notes: Keep Day 1 relaxed to recover from travel. The Metro Red Line from the airport connects easily to the city center. Validate your Viva Viagem card (€0.50) and load it with credit for the week — saves money over single tickets. Time Out Market is open until midnight, so no rush.

day_by_day.morning: Start with the Alfama Historic District Walking Tour — Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood. A guided tour through narrow medieval alleyways reveals Moorish heritage, colorful tiled buildings, and hidden miradouros (viewpoints). Tours typically begin around 10:00 and last 2–2.5 hours.
day_by_day.afternoon: Transition directly into the São Jorge Castle and Mouraria Exploration. Perched atop Alfama's highest hill, the 11th-century Moorish castle offers sweeping panoramic views over Lisbon and the Tagus. Explore the ramparts, towers, and the archaeological site within. Afterward, descend into the Mouraria quarter — Lisbon's multicultural heart — for a wander through its vibrant streets.
day_by_day.evening: Return to the Bairro Alto or Chiado area for dinner. Enjoy a sit-down meal at a traditional tasca (Portuguese tavern) with dishes like caldo verde soup, grilled sea bream, or slow-cooked lamb. End the evening with a glass of ginjinha (cherry liqueur) at one of the old-school ginjinha bars near Largo de São Domingos.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel or at a neighborhood café — galão (milky coffee) with toast and eggs (€4–7).
meals.lunch: Quick lunch in Alfama after the tour — try a tasca near the Sé Cathedral for a prato do dia (dish of the day) with wine, typically €10–13.
meals.dinner: Traditional tasca in Bairro Alto — 2-course meal with wine around €20–28 per person. Try Taberna da Rua das Flores or similar mid-range spots.

day_by_day.notes: Book the Alfama Walking Tour in advance online — Sunday tours fill up quickly. São Jorge Castle entry is around €15; get there before 14:00 to avoid peak crowds. Wear comfortable walking shoes — Alfama's cobblestones are steep and uneven.

day_by_day.morning: Dedicate the morning to the Belém waterfront district. Take Tram 15E or the bus from Praça do Comércio (about 20 minutes). Visit the iconic 16th-century Belém Tower (Torre de Belém) and the magnificent Jerónimos Monastery — masterpieces of Manueline architecture celebrating Portugal's Age of Discovery. Arrive early (around 09:30) to beat the crowds.
day_by_day.afternoon: After the monuments, make a pilgrimage to the original Pastéis de Belém bakery (open since 1837) for the world-famous custard tarts straight from the oven, dusted with cinnamon. Spend the rest of the afternoon exploring the Belém Cultural Centre area or strolling along the Tagus riverside promenade. Optionally visit the free Monument to the Discoveries.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon. Explore the upscale Príncipe Real neighborhood — browse its antique shops and independent boutiques. Dine at a wine-focused restaurant in Príncipe Real, pairing Portuguese natural wines with creative petiscos (small plates). This neighborhood offers excellent mid-range dining with a local crowd.

meals.breakfast: Early breakfast at the hotel before heading to Belém.
meals.lunch: Pastéis de Belém custard tarts (€1.50 each) plus a light lunch at a riverside café in Belém — grilled sardine sandwich or a soup and salad (€10–15).
meals.dinner: Petiscos and wine bar in Príncipe Real — expect €25–35 per person with drinks. Try Taberna da Rua das Flores or Wine with Spirit.

day_by_day.notes: Jerónimos Monastery is closed on Mondays in some periods — verify opening times before visiting and consider rearranging with Day 4 if needed. Belém Tower and Monastery combined tickets can save money. Book Belém tickets online to skip queues.

day_by_day.morning: Take a morning ride on the historic Tram 28 through Lisbon's hilly neighborhoods — a quintessential Lisbon experience passing through Graça, Alfama, and Estrela. Hop off at Miradouro da Graça for one of the city's best panoramic views, especially beautiful in morning light. Explore the Graça neighborhood's local market and quiet streets.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — a must for history lovers, housed in a former 16th-century convent. The collection traces the story of Portugal's iconic azulejo tiles from the 15th century to the present, including a stunning 23-meter panoramic tile panel of pre-earthquake Lisbon (1755). Allow 2 hours.
day_by_day.evening: Experience the Traditional Fado Dinner in Bairro Alto — the emotional soul of Portugal. Enjoy a set menu dinner at a traditional casa de fado with live Fado performances throughout the evening. This is a highlight of any Lisbon trip and a deeply moving cultural experience.

meals.breakfast: Café breakfast in Graça neighborhood — fresh bread, cheese, ham, and coffee at a local pastelaria (€5–8).
meals.lunch: Light lunch near the Tile Museum or back in Alfama — a simple prato do dia at a neighborhood restaurant (€10–14).
meals.dinner: Traditional Fado Dinner in Bairro Alto — set menu typically €35–50 per person including food, wine, and the Fado show. Book well in advance.

day_by_day.notes: Tram 28 is extremely popular — go early (before 09:30) to avoid long queues and get a seat. The Fado dinner reservation is essential — book at least 1–2 weeks ahead. Most casas de fado have a minimum spend policy; confirm when booking. Dress smart-casual for the Fado experience.

day_by_day.morning: Spend a relaxed final morning at the Mercado de Campo de Ourique — a beloved local neighborhood market beloved by Lisboetas. Browse fresh produce, local cheeses, charcuterie, and artisan goods. Have a leisurely breakfast at one of the market's cafés. Afterward, explore the charming Estrela neighborhood and visit the beautiful Jardim da Estrela (Estrela Garden) for a peaceful morning stroll.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Chiado and Baixa for last-minute souvenir shopping — pick up local olive oil, wine, tinned fish (conservas), or azulejo tiles. Visit the historic Livraria Bertrand (world's oldest operating bookshop, founded 1732) in Chiado. Take one final walk along Rua Augusta and Praça do Comércio for photos by the Tagus River.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner at a classic Portuguese restaurant in Chiado or Baixa. Splurge slightly on a memorable last meal — bacalhau à brás (shredded salted cod with eggs and potatoes), arroz de marisco (seafood rice), or grilled black pork. Toast to Lisbon with a glass of Vinho Verde or a local craft beer.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at Mercado de Campo de Ourique — fresh pastries, fruit, and a galão (€6–10).
meals.lunch: Light lunch in Chiado — a bifana (pork sandwich) or soup at a traditional café (€7–12).
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at a well-regarded mid-range restaurant in Chiado — €30–40 per person with wine. Consider Solar dos Presuntos or Cervejaria Ramiro (slightly upscale but iconic for seafood).

day_by_day.notes: If your departure flight is on May 20 or later, this evening is perfect for a relaxed goodbye to Lisbon. If flying out early on May 20, pack bags the night before and confirm airport transfer time. Keep some euros for last-minute purchases. Conservas (tinned fish) make excellent, TSA-friendly souvenirs.

Visit the iconic Livraria Bertrand, the world's oldest operating bookshop, for a cultural first impression.

Enjoy a curated set menu of Portuguese classics paired with fine regional wines while being serenaded by the haunting, soulful melodies of Portugal's most beloved musical tradition. A perfect and emotionally resonant introduction to Lisbon's culture.

meals.breakfast: Enjoy a welcome snack or light refreshment upon hotel arrival — the hotel's concierge can arrange a curated in-room Portuguese charcuterie and pastry board with local cheeses, presunto, and a bottle of Vinho Verde.
meals.lunch: Late lunch at Alma (Michelin-starred, Chef Henrique Sá Pessoa) in Chiado — indulge in refined modern Portuguese cuisine with a tasting menu celebrating seasonal, locally sourced ingredients.
meals.dinner: Included as part of the Traditional Fado Dinner experience in Bairro Alto — a set menu featuring dishes such as bacalhau à brás, caldo verde soup, and classic Portuguese desserts like arroz doce.

day_by_day.notes: Arrival day is intentionally relaxed. Request a late check-in guarantee from the hotel in advance. The Fado dinner reservation should be pre-booked; typical shows begin around 20:00–21:00. Dress code is smart casual to elegant.

day_by_day.morning: Alfama Historic District Walking Tour — Begin the day with a guided private walking tour through Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood. Wind through narrow medieval alleyways, discover hidden miradouros (viewpoints), visit the Sé Cathedral, and learn about the Moorish, Visigoth, and Roman layers of history embedded in every cobblestone. The morning light on the terracotta rooftops is spectacular.
day_by_day.afternoon: São Jorge Castle and Mouraria Exploration — Continue uphill to the 11th-century Moorish castle perched atop Lisbon's highest hill. Explore the ancient ramparts, towers, and archaeological site within the castle grounds, and enjoy sweeping panoramic views over the Tagus River and the city's red-roofed skyline. Afterward, descend into the vibrant Mouraria quarter, the historic Moorish district, for a cultural walkthrough.
day_by_day.evening: Return to the hotel to freshen up, then enjoy a sunset cocktail at a rooftop bar such as TOPO Chiado or Sky Bar at Tivoli Avenida Liberdade, offering breathtaking views over the city as the golden hour light bathes Lisbon's hills.

meals.breakfast: Luxury breakfast at the hotel — expect a full spread of fresh pastries, Portuguese cheeses, smoked fish, fresh fruit, and freshly brewed coffee or tea.
meals.lunch: Picturesque lunch at Chapitô à Mesa, a beloved Alfama restaurant with stunning terrace views over the city and a creative Portuguese menu featuring dishes like grilled octopus and seasonal vegetable risotto.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Bica do Sapato, a design-forward riverside restaurant in Santa Apolónia offering modern Portuguese cuisine with exceptional river views — try the tasting menu with wine pairing for a full premium experience.

day_by_day.notes: Wear comfortable walking shoes — Alfama's cobblestones can be uneven. A private guide for the morning walking tour is strongly recommended for deeper historical context. Book São Jorge Castle tickets in advance to skip queues.

day_by_day.morning: Belém Tower, Jerónimos Monastery & Pastéis de Belém — Take a private chauffeured transfer to the historic Belém waterfront district. Begin with the iconic 16th-century Belém Tower, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and masterpiece of Manueline architecture standing guard over the Tagus. Then visit the breathtaking Jerónimos Monastery, one of Portugal's most magnificent Gothic-Manueline monuments, built to celebrate Vasco da Gama's voyage to India.
day_by_day.afternoon: After the monastery, stop at the legendary Pastéis de Belém bakery — the original home of the pastel de nata (custard tart), made to a secret recipe since 1837. Enjoy warm tarts dusted with cinnamon and powdered sugar. Then visit the MAAT (Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology) along the riverside for a contemporary cultural contrast to the morning's historic grandeur.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and enjoy a relaxed evening exploring the elegant Príncipe Real neighborhood — browse antique shops, visit the weekend garden market, and enjoy aperitivo hour at a sophisticated wine bar.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel before departure to Belém.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Feitoria, a Michelin-starred restaurant inside the Altis Belém Hotel & Spa, offering a refined tasting menu of contemporary Portuguese cuisine with stunning views over the Tagus River — one of Lisbon's most prestigious dining experiences.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Tasca do Chico in Madragoa — an intimate, reservation-essential restaurant celebrated for its authentic petiscos (Portuguese tapas), exceptional wine list, and warm, neighborhood atmosphere. A true hidden gem of Lisbon's food scene.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is approximately 6–7 km from central Lisbon. A private transfer is recommended for comfort. Book Jerónimos Monastery and Feitoria well in advance, especially on weekends. The Pastéis de Belém bakery may have a queue — arrive early or enjoy takeaway tarts at the riverside.

day_by_day.morning: Private guided tour of the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — Discover the extraordinary 500-year history of Portugal's iconic azulejo ceramic tiles in this stunning museum housed within a 16th-century convent. Marvel at the 23-meter panoramic tile panel depicting pre-earthquake Lisbon (circa 1700s) and explore exquisite galleries of hand-painted tilework. A deeply immersive cultural and historical experience unique to Portugal.
day_by_day.afternoon: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Experience — Spend a curated afternoon at Lisbon's iconic food hall in Cais do Sodré, sampling the very best of Portuguese cuisine under one roof. From Michelin-starred chef counters to artisan gelato, fresh seafood, ginjinha, and regional wines — this is an unparalleled culinary journey. Stroll along the nearby Ribeira waterfront afterward and enjoy the riverside ambiance.
day_by_day.evening: Sunset at Miradouro da Graça — one of Lisbon's most romantic and less-touristy viewpoints — followed by a private wine tasting experience at a premium Lisbon wine cellar such as Garrafeira Nacional or a curated session at By the Wine, exploring the finest Douro, Alentejo, and Dão region wines.

meals.lunch: Grazing lunch at Time Out Market — sample highlights such as fresh Atlantic prawns, bifanas (pork sandwiches), pastéis de bacalhau (salt cod fritters), and a glass of chilled Vinho Verde. Budget €30–50 per person for a generous spread.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Belcanto, Chef José Avillez's two-Michelin-starred flagship restaurant in Chiado — widely considered Lisbon's finest dining experience. The tasting menu 'Descobertas' (Discoveries) reimagines Portuguese culinary heritage through avant-garde technique. Reserve months in advance.

day_by_day.notes: Belcanto is one of the most sought-after reservations in Lisbon — book as early as possible, ideally 2–3 months ahead. Smart dress is expected. The National Tile Museum is best visited on weekday mornings when it is quieter. Request a private docent guide for the museum for the best experience.

day_by_day.morning: Sintra Day Trip (Optional Upgrade) or Lisbon Leisure Morning — For those wishing to explore beyond the city, a private chauffeured excursion to the UNESCO-listed fairy-tale town of Sintra (40 minutes from Lisbon) is highly recommended. Visit Pena Palace, perched dramatically above the clouds, and the enchanting Quinta da Regaleira with its mysterious Initiation Well. Alternatively, enjoy a slow, luxurious morning in Lisbon — visit the Gulbenkian Museum's world-class art collection or browse the elegant Avenida da Liberdade for Portuguese luxury brands.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Lisbon (if visiting Sintra) and enjoy a final leisurely afternoon in the Príncipe Real and Santos districts. Visit the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) for a final dose of Portuguese art history, housing masterworks including Nuno Gonçalves' iconic Panels of St. Vincent. Afterward, indulge in a luxury spa session at the hotel or a nearby premium wellness center.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner celebrating the end of a magnificent Lisbon journey — a final evening of Portuguese elegance and gastronomy.

meals.breakfast: Leisurely breakfast at the hotel — take your time and savor the full spread on your final morning.
meals.lunch: If in Sintra: lunch at Incomum by Luis Santos, a refined restaurant in Sintra town center with creative regional cuisine and a celebrated wine list. If staying in Lisbon: lunch at Eleven, a Michelin-starred restaurant with panoramic city views from Eduardo VII Park.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at Varanda Restaurant at Four Seasons Hotel Ritz Lisbon — an iconic Lisbon institution offering impeccable classic Portuguese and international cuisine in a grand, sophisticated setting with live piano. Alternatively, reserve at Loco (one Michelin star) for an adventurous, avant-garde Portuguese tasting menu that pushes culinary boundaries in the most memorable way.

day_by_day.notes: If flying home the next morning, confirm hotel late checkout or luggage storage options. Pack the night before to ensure a relaxed final evening. Consider purchasing artisan souvenirs such as hand-painted azulejo tiles, premium cork goods, or bottles of aged Moscatel de Setúbal from a specialty shop before departure.
